# Draft translation

A sentence-by-sentence draft of the booklet, built on [glossary.md](./glossary.md).
Nothing here is confirmed by the author.

How to read it:

- Plain words follow the glossary. Many of those rest on a few contexts only, so check
  the glossary's confidence column before relying on a word.
- **[Bracketed]** words are guesses from context or from the picture: either the word is
  not in the glossary, or its glossary entry is too weak to lean on. Treat them as
  placeholders that fit, not as readings. There are about three per sentence.
- **[...]** marks a stretch that cannot be read yet.
- English word order has been restored; the booklet puts the verb first.
- Names such as Ktbew or Ctvork are the transcript's arbitrary letters, not pronunciations.

Sentences are numbered section.sentence, in the order of the
[transcript](./transcript/joined_text.txt). The drafts are kept in
[decipherment/translations.tsv](./decipherment/translations.tsv), one row per sentence.

## 10. The rope, and the conclusion (pages 19-21)

Picture: Five pieces of cord; a figure in a well reaching for a rope knotted from different cords; the walker again, on another broken arcade.

**10.0** *rt hrnr sior stsa liotga nrsi leb est ltsr maaoise dtbwei otkdt leb uamrb.*

> The woman did as the [stranger] told her, and [when] she tied all the lost [ends] together, [she had] at last a long rope that she lowered into the well.

**10.7** *he me ctheui oe dtbwei he giprlev.*

> And so the child [was] saved, and lived.

**10.8** *laoab rt nene stsa rtwe wt oi leb liotga nrsi oe awrlr ade.*

> This old tale is said to be a [parable] of the Scattered Path.

**10.9** *wi meuek oi iur oe ctge nena ifa hrkga twt ueni gehi utyt.*

> The truth that will [bind] them in one piece may not be found.

**10.10** *nae dta oe mrue nrsi oeur wiua weoege oa oe est ueni oe rtwe ctfe oe paksewa intburse nrsi oe efet he oe crgi hrca oe yie figise nrsi oe fectweb hrca oe yawi faptse nrsi oe hepe hrca oe dtht fatpt grut nrsi oe cibe hrca oe utdali iase nrsi oe ktbew hrca oe ioise nrsi oe eltprw hrca oe mrue nena livpe yanr oe oafr nrsi oe avotft hrca oe lilr dtntkdt nrsi oe ctvork.*

> For the [ends] of rope tied together by the woman in the tale are like the linked volumes of the Efet and the Crgi, or the window scrolls of the Fectweb, or the tomb [candlesticks] of the Hepe, or the [far] broken road of the Cibe, or the [carved] stones of the Ktbew, or the shards of the Eltprw, or the [ones] that [lie] [across] the [grounds] of the Avotft, or the [high] bridges of the Ctvork.

**10.11** *medtk ce ekrot oe dabwese nrsi ytoa fidesise wrut leb crlrye wia leb crlrye dabwegt rda tla iyi cipa nrsi oeur wt dane sior neekmr sihrye he sawrut deme.*

> Can we [weave] the [strands] of these traditions into a larger whole, a larger story, as [so many] [short] lengths of rope, to form another [much] longer and [stronger] cord?

**10.12** *nae esa meuek ytge oe ctgese nahame mahiga he ae wt tnt oa cesanase ntoagt hayr hrca stuahi wt hayr oe wi dane nrsi utmase.*

> [Unclear:] For not all the truths have already [been] joined, and some [...] to work by humans [...], or [give] thought to [...] the true form of things.

**10.13** *eur dta ytge oe lesi nrsi laurrse yarhe yrena twt gaet htlr wt oi mahiga.*

> But all the remains of [...] are visible around them, [waiting] only to be joined.
